title: Chapter VII
focus: the first death and growing guilt

teacherSummary.text: A letter from his father reports that Victor's youngest brother, William, has been murdered. Returning to Geneva during a storm, Victor glimpses the creature near the spot and becomes certain it is the killer. He learns that Justine has been accused because William's locket was found on her.

vocabulary.definition: A one-horse carriage with two seats and a calash top
vocabulary.context: But now, as soon as the horses arrived, I hurried into a cabriolet, and bade farewell to my friend.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cabriolet”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Is this to prognosticate peace, or to mock at my unhappiness?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “prognosticate”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + gnos (Greek gnosis, "knowledge") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Adapted for removing scales, as from a fish
vocabulary.context: Who could arrest a creature capable of scaling the overhanging sides of Mont Salêve?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “scaling”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: One sudden and desolating change had taken place; but a thousand little circumstances might have by degrees worked other alterations, which, although they were done more tranquilly, might not be the less decisive.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “desolate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + sol (Latin solus, "alone" / sol, "sun") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: “Come, Victor; not brooding thoughts of vengeance against the assassin, but with feelings of peace and gentleness, that will heal, instead of festering, the wounds of our minds.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fester”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: That can not be removed, washed away, blotted out, or effaced
vocabulary.context: Six years had elapsed, passed as a dream but for one indelible trace, and I stood in the same place where I had last embraced my father before my departure for Ingolstadt.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “indelible”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ible (Latin -ibilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Flesh of slain animals or men
vocabulary.context: I had turned loose into the world a depraved wretch, whose delight was in carnage and misery; had he not murdered my brother?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “carnage”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: I well knew that if any other had communicated such a relation to me, I should have looked upon it as the ravings of insanity.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “raving”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Reliance on the truth of something said or done
vocabulary.context: Besides, the strange nature of the animal would elude all pursuit, even if I were so far credited as to persuade my relatives to commence it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “credit”: cred (Latin credere, "to believe"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: One who kills, or attempts to kill, by surprise or secret assault
vocabulary.context: “Come, Victor; not brooding thoughts of vengeance against the assassin, but with feelings of peace and gentleness, that will heal, instead of festering, the wounds of our minds.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “assassin”: as- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: The Alps and storms are classic sublime settings—vast nature that inspires awe and fear.

significance: Victor's silence begins here: he knows the truth but says nothing, making him complicit.
discussionQuestions: Should Victor tell the authorities what he knows? Why does he stay silent?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VII,” how does Shelley show the first death and growing guilt? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter VII, how does Shelley develop the idea of the first death and growing guilt? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VII develops the idea of the first death and growing guilt. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter VII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of the first death and growing guilt. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter VII suggests about the first death and growing guilt. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and imagery), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter VII to complicate the reader's understanding of the first death and growing guilt. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the first death and growing guilt responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter VII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the first death and growing guilt follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter VII and its treatment of the first death and growing guilt. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and imagery, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter VII as evidence for a larger claim about the first death and growing guilt in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the first death and growing guilt. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events
annotationFocus.passage: “Come, Victor; not brooding thoughts of vengeance against the assassin, but with feelings of peace and gentleness, that will heal, instead of festering, the wounds of our minds. Enter the house of mourning, my friend, but with kindness and affection for those who love you, and not with hatred for your enemies.

annotationFocus.label: Imagery
annotationFocus.lookFor: sensory details (sight, sound, cold, light) and what mood they create

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Should Victor tell the authorities what he knows? Why does he stay silent? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are cabriolet, prognosticate, scaling, desolating, festering. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “But now, as soon as the horses arrived, I hurried into a cabriolet, and bade farewell to my friend.” Webster's says: A one-horse carriage with two seats and a calash top. Now the word history: “cabriolet”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “prognosticate”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + gnos (Greek gnosis, "knowledge") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “scaling”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The Alps and storms are classic sublime settings—vast nature that inspires awe and fear. Why does this chapter matter? Victor's silence begins here: he knows the truth but says nothing, making him complicit. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the first death and growing guilt.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Imagery, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “Come, Victor; not brooding thoughts of vengeance against the assassin, but with feelings of peace and gentleness, that will heal, instead of festering, the wounds of our minds. Enter the house of mourning, my friend, but with kindness and affection for those who love you, and not with hatred for your enemies.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Imagery, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter VII,” how does Shelley show the first death and growing guilt? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the first death and growing guilt, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes the first death and growing guilt. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
